nameStory: The Mediterranean House Gecko gets its name from its Mediterranean homeland and its love of living in and around human homes. It's also called the Turkish gecko, reflecting its abundance in Turkey, and the charming nickname 'moon lizard' because it emerges to hunt when the moon rises.
description: This small, nocturnal gecko is a recent arrival to New England, having spread from its Mediterranean origins to many parts of the world. It rarely grows longer than 6 inches and has the distinctive gecko features of large, unblinking eyes with vertical pupils and sticky toe pads. Its skin appears purple-gray or tan with dark spots, and if you look closely, you can actually see through its translucent belly to glimpse its internal organs.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, lidless eyes with vertical, cat-like pupils that appear almost otherworldly in flashlight beams. The eyes feel smooth and glassy if gently touched, never closing like other lizards.

idTips.label: Toe Pads
idTips.description: Expanded, sticky toe pads that feel slightly tacky to the touch, allowing the gecko to walk up smooth glass and walls with ease. Each toe spreads wide like tiny hands.

idTips.label: Pattern
idTips.description: Purple-gray or tan skin covered with irregular black or dark brown spots, often forming bands across the tail. The belly appears ghostly translucent, sometimes revealing dark internal structures.

idTips.label: Scales
idTips.description: Small, granular scales that feel like fine sandpaper when stroked gently. Unlike snakes, the scales don't overlap but create a pebbly texture across the entire body.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Compact body rarely exceeding 6 inches total length, with about half that length being the segmented tail. Fits easily in the palm of your hand.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Strictly nocturnal, most active around 2 AM. Often found motionless on walls or ceilings during the day, becoming animated only after dark when hunting insects.

habitat: In New England, Mediterranean House Geckos are found almost exclusively in and around heated human structures like homes, greenhouses, and commercial buildings. They require warm environments year-round and take shelter in wall cracks, behind siding, or in basements. The few New England sightings have been in urban areas, likely near ports or garden centers where they arrived as stowaways.

seasonality.spring: May emerge from winter hiding spots in heated buildings as temperatures warm. Look for them on interior walls of warm structures during evening hours.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they may venture outdoors on warm nights. Check exterior walls of buildings near outdoor lighting where insects congregate.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as temperatures drop, retreating deeper into heated buildings. Late fall sightings become rare except in consistently warm indoor spaces.
seasonality.winter: Essentially inactive in New England's cold climate, surviving only in heated indoor environments like basements, greenhouses, or warm commercial buildings.

funFact: Mediterranean House Geckos can walk upside-down across your ceiling thanks to millions of microscopic hairs on their toe pads that use molecular forces to stick to any surface - even smooth glass - yet they can instantly release their grip to dart away from danger.
confusionNotes: In New England, these are unlikely to be confused with native species due to their unique toe pads and nocturnal habits. The translucent belly and ability to climb smooth surfaces immediately distinguishes them from any native lizard or salamander.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'Mediterranean,' these geckos have become so associated with human habitation worldwide that they're considered commensal species - animals that live alongside humans. In their native range, they're considered good luck and are welcomed in homes as natural pest controllers.
compareHints: Mediterranean House Geckos are the most likely of the Hemidactylus genus to survive in New England's climate due to their cold tolerance and association with heated buildings. Unlike the Tropical House Gecko which prefers consistently warm climates, or the Indo-Pacific House Gecko found mainly in tropical ports, the Mediterranean species has proven more adaptable to temperate regions with human-provided shelter.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The tropical house gecko is larger and more robust than its relative the Mediterranean house gecko, with a chunkier build and more pronounced toe pads.
Compared to its close cousin the Mediterranean House Gecko, the Indo-Pacific species has more pronounced spiny scales along the tail edges and tends to be slightly smaller overall.
